passage:
Mentor's note, animation institute, Monday
Anirban (19) came to my desk again today to say the course is 'excellent, the best in the country'. It's the third time this month, and nobody had asked. His family paid the full fee upfront; he told me his father sold a plot of land for it. The same week, three of his batchmates complained that the software lab has been down for six weeks and two faculty members have left. When I asked Anirban how he felt about the lab, he said, 'It doesn't matter, the name is what counts.' His hands were tight around his bag strap. I didn't argue. I said he could tell me the good and the bad here, and nobody would think less of him or his family. He said nothing, but he stayed another ten minutes. I'll check in with him on Friday.
Jeevan

qa.q: How long has the software lab been down?
qa.a: The software lab has been down for six weeks.

qa.q: What do Anirban's tight hands suggest?
qa.a: They suggest tension under the praise: Anirban may have doubts about the course, but with his father's land sold to pay for it, admitting doubt feels too costly.

qa.q: Why was Jeevan's choice not to argue a good one?
qa.a: Arguing might make Anirban defend the course harder; offering a safe place to say the good and the bad gives him room to admit doubts in his own time.

qa.q: How might Anirban's batchmates see his praise of the course?
qa.a: The batchmates, who complained about the lab and faculty, may find it puzzling or frustrating, since they are living with the same problems.

grounding: Shows a mentor's note on a student whose family paid heavily for a disappointing course, who keeps calling it excellent and brushes aside its problems.

passage:
Thursday night
Parveen Api called again and asked if I'm happy at the hotel management college. I said yes, very. It's true. It is a great course. Okay, the 'international internship' turned out to be a hotel in our own city, and half the classes are videos from 2015. But the campus is nice, and the fees were high for a reason. Abbu took a loan for this. Four lakh. That has to mean something. Api said Rafia's college is half the price and they already have kitchen practice. I told her that's a different level. I didn't tell her I've been sitting in the library during class because the lecturer just reads the slides. Whatever. I'm not leaving. People who leave are quitters. I'll make it worth it.
Imran

qa.a: Abbu took a loan of four lakh.

qa.q: Why does Imran say 'That has to mean something' about the high fees?
qa.a: Imran feels the pressure of Abbu's four-lakh loan and is anxious for the course to be worth it, so the cost itself starts to feel like proof of quality.

qa.q: What small step could help Imran look at the course more honestly?
qa.a: Imran could write down privately what the course has actually delivered against what was promised, and talk it over with Api without deciding anything yet.

qa.q: How might Parveen Api feel hearing 'that's a different level'?
qa.a: Api may feel worried and a bit shut out, sensing that Imran is unhappy but defending the course too hard to talk about it.

grounding: Shows a student in a diary insisting a costly course is great despite broken promises, because the money spent makes doubt hard to admit.

passage:
In Sikar, the coaching institute for government exams had a big glass front and a banner of smiling toppers. Akash's father had sold a piece of farmland to pay the fee: one full year, paid in advance.

Four months in, classes were packed with two hundred students, the good teacher had left, and the new one read from the book. Akash's mock test scores had gone down.

His sister Jahnavi, home for Holi, looked through his notes. "Akash, you said last month that the doubt sessions were cancelled. And the teacher who you liked left. Why not try the free online lectures and the library instead?"

"No," Akash said sharply. "It's the best institute in Sikar. Everyone says so. The system just takes time."

"Your scores went down."

"That's me, not them. The institute is excellent."

He didn't say what he was thinking: Papa sold the land for this. It has to be worth it.

qa.q: What did Akash's father sell to pay the fee?
qa.a: A piece of farmland.

qa.q: Why does Akash insist the institute is excellent, even as his scores go down?
qa.a: His father sold land to pay for it, so admitting it's disappointing would feel like wasting that sacrifice. The more that was invested, the harder it is to doubt.

qa.q: What could help Akash look at the choice more honestly without feeling he has failed Papa?
qa.a: He could list what is and isn't working and talk with Jahnavi or Papa about adding the library and free lectures. Changing course to do better isn't wasting the land.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel when Akash blames himself instead of the institute?
qa.a: Jahnavi may feel worried and frustrated, since she can see the cancelled sessions and the teacher leaving. She wants to help, but his defensiveness makes it hard.

grounding: A student whose father sold land for an expensive coaching institute insists it is excellent despite falling scores, finding it too costly to admit doubt.

passage:
In their shared flat in Warsaw, Marek found Bilal at the kitchen table at midnight, editing a short film alone on his laptop.

"Isn't that supposed to be done in the studio at your course?"

"The studio's booked," Bilal said. "It's fine."

It had been booked for three weeks. Bilal had paid the full year's fee for the private film academy, most of his savings from two summers of work, because the website promised industry mentors and professional cameras. So far, two mentor sessions had been cancelled and the cameras were older than Marek's phone.

"You could ask for part of the fee back," Marek said. "Or switch to the public course next term."

"Switch?" Bilal shut the laptop. "It's one of the best academies in the country. The cancellations are temporary. I'm lucky to be there."

"You were complaining about it yesterday."

"I was tired." Bilal stood up. "It's excellent. I'm not leaving."

qa.q: What had the website promised?
qa.a: Industry mentors and professional cameras.

qa.q: Why does Bilal call himself lucky to be at the academy after complaining yesterday?
qa.a: He spent most of two summers' savings on it, so admitting disappointment would feel like admitting a costly mistake. Insisting it's excellent protects him from that feeling.

qa.q: What could Bilal do to consider his options without feeling foolish?
qa.a: He could write down what the academy promised and what he has received, then look calmly at choices like asking about fees or switching next term. Treating it as new information, not a personal failure, makes change easier.

qa.q: How might Marek feel after Bilal shuts the laptop and walks away?
qa.a: Marek might feel shut out and worried, since he can see his friend editing alone at midnight. Marek may decide not to raise it again, despite caring.

grounding: A student who spent most of his savings on a disappointing film academy insists it is excellent and refuses to consider leaving.

Tuesday
Another animation class where the trainer played a video for two hours and left. Chaitanya asked me again at lunch if I'm sure about this institute. I said yes, obviously. It's one of the best in the city. Everyone says so. Well, the brochure says so.
Papa paid the full year's fee in one go. Nani added money from her bangles too. So it HAS to be good. If it weren't, what would that make me? Someone who wasted all that. No. The software they use is industry standard. The building is nice. The certificate will look good.
Chaitanya said the government polytechnic course has actual teachers. I told him that's for people who can't afford better. I don't know why I said that. It came out meaner than I meant.
I'm tired. Going to watch the tutorial video again.
Ankita

qa.a: The trainer played a video for two hours and left.

qa.a: Ankita feels uneasy and a little guilty about what the family paid, so admitting doubt would feel like admitting waste, and defending the choice eases that tension.

passage: At the bus stand in Sangli, Aparna waited with her brother Akash for the evening bus to Miraj. 'How's the diploma?' she asked. He had joined the private computer institute above the cloth market in June; their father had sold two goats and borrowed from their uncle for the fee. 'Excellent,' Akash said quickly. 'Best in the district.' 'But you said the lab computers don't switch on.' 'They're fixing them.' 'And the sir who comes only twice a week?' 'He's very experienced. He teaches in Kolhapur also.' Aparna looked at him. 'The polytechnic takes admissions again in January. Rajesh from our lane goes there.' Akash's jaw tightened. 'After everything Baba paid? I'm not leaving. It's a good course.' The bus came. He climbed on first and didn't talk until Miraj.

Lindiwe had paid the whole fee for the private animation academy in Cape Town in one go, using savings from two years of weekend work. By October the classes were half empty, two tutors had left, and the software licences still hadn't arrived.

"It's still the best course in the country," Lindiwe told her friend Rania over coffee. "The self-study is actually good for discipline. And the certificate will look great."

"You said you haven't touched the software in six weeks."
"That's temporary. Everyone says it'll be fixed."
"Who's everyone?"

Lindiwe stirred her coffee harder. "Look, I'm not dropping it. I put everything into this."

Rania didn't push. But she noticed that every time Lindiwe listed the course's strengths, the list got longer and her voice got higher.

qa.a: Lindiwe feels disappointed but has put two years of savings in, so admitting doubt feels too painful, and defending it eases that tension.

passage:
At the coaching institute in Kota, the glossy brochure had promised small batches and top teachers. Ayesha's family had paid the full year's fee in April. By July her batch had ninety students, the famous physics teacher had left, and the doubt sessions were always "cancelled today".

Nitin, from her hostel, had switched to self-study with an online course. "It's working better for me," he said.

"You gave up too early," Ayesha said. "This institute is still the best. Big batches are good for competition. And the new teacher is... fine."

"You said you didn't understand a single lecture this week."

"That's my fault, not theirs."

Nitin shrugged. That night Ayesha opened her notebook to list the things the institute had done well. She wrote three. Then she sat looking at the empty lines beneath for a long time.

qa.q: How many students were in Ayesha's batch by July?
qa.a: Ayesha's batch had ninety students.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha say not understanding the lectures was her fault?
qa.a: Ayesha felt disappointed, but her family had paid a lot, so blaming herself felt easier than admitting doubt about the institute.

qa.q: What could Ayesha do with her doubts?
qa.a: She could talk honestly with her parents and a counsellor about what the institute is and isn't giving her, and look at the options.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel when Ayesha says he gave up too early?
qa.a: Nitin might feel slightly stung, but mostly concerned, seeing her defend something that isn't working for her.

grounding: Shows a student whose family paid a large fee for a disappointing coaching institute, and who defends it against her own doubts.

Dear Hafsa,

You asked how the online MBA is going. It's going great, honestly. I know it cost a lot, more than my first year's salary, but it's world-class. Yes, the live classes turned into recorded videos. Yes, the "personal mentor" has replied to me once in four months. And yes, the alumni network turned out to be a chat group of forty people who mostly post memes.

But that's how online courses are. And I'm learning discipline. Everyone says the certificate opens doors. I'd be foolish to quit after paying so much, right?

Anyway, I'm definitely not thinking about leaving. I've barely even looked at the refund policy. Well, twice.

How are you? Tell me about your new job.

Divyansh

qa.a: The mentor has replied once in four months.

qa.q: Why does Divyansh insist the course is world-class?
qa.a: Divyansh feels disappointed and doubtful but has invested so much that admitting it hurts, so defending the course eases the tension.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do to look at the choice more honestly?
qa.a: Divyansh could list what the course has actually delivered, read the refund policy properly, and talk it through with Hafsa or a trusted adviser.

qa.a: Hafsa may notice the doubts slipping through, like reading the refund policy twice, and gently ask how Divyansh really feels.

passage: Chinmay, you asked why I stayed in that coaching institute so long. I'm Sunaina, and honestly, it's embarrassing. My parents paid a huge fee for the one-year entrance coaching in Kota. Everyone said it was the best. By month two I knew the teachers read from slides and never answered doubts. The batch had three hundred students. But whenever anyone asked, I said, "It's excellent. Week 1. Sumit started the animation diploma that had cost his family a big share of their savings. He posted photos from the first day. "Best institute in the city!"
Week 4. The software licences hadn't arrived. Two teachers had quit. Sumit told his friend Jaya, "It's still the best course. These are just small problems." Jaya asked, "Are you learning anything?" "Of course. It's excellent." But he spent most classes watching videos on his own laptop.
Week 9. Jaya showed him a free online course that covered more than his diploma had so far. Sumit got angry. "That's not the same. Mine is professional." That night, he lay awake doing sums. If he left now, all that money was gone. If he stayed, maybe it would get better. Next morning, he messaged Jaya: "Maybe it's not excellent. I don't know what to do." Jaya replied: "Let's talk to your parents together. And ask the institute for a refund policy."

qa.q: What had not arrived by Week 4?
qa.a: The software licences hadn't arrived.

qa.q: Why did Sumit get angry when Jaya showed him the free course?
qa.a: Sumit felt defensive and guilty about the money already spent, so any doubt about the diploma was hard to face.

qa.q: What sensible steps did Jaya suggest?
qa.a: Talking to his parents together and asking the institute about its refund policy, so the decision is shared and informed.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel watching Sumit defend the course for weeks?
qa.a: Jaya was probably worried and patient, waiting for Sumit to be ready to admit his doubts.

passage: Varun, you're defending that hotel management course like it's your own child. Let your Avni Mausi tell you something. When I was twenty, I joined a fashion diploma in Delhi. The fee was huge. My father sold his scooter for the first term. In the first month I knew the teachers barely came, and the sewing machines didn't work. Rain had knocked out the power in their Chennai hostel for the second night that monsoon, and Nikita and Leela sat on the floor with a phone torch between them. The refund form for Nikita's weekend design course had to be submitted by nine the next morning.
"You said yourself the tutor skipped two classes and just reads slides," Leela said.
"That's his style. It's a premium course; the fees were huge for a reason. The certificate alone is worth it."
"You've learnt more from the free videos you watch at night."
"Those don't count." Nikita clicked the torch off, then on. "I've put six months of savings into this. If it's bad, then I was stupid, and I wasn't. It's excellent. I'm staying."
The form stayed blank on the screen until the battery died.

qa.q: By when did the refund form have to be submitted?
qa.a: By nine the next morning.

qa.q: Why does Nikita insist the course is excellent?
qa.a: Nikita feels anxious and defensive: admitting the course is weak would mean feeling foolish about six months of savings, so praising it protects Nikita's pride.

qa.q: What could help Nikita decide more clearly?
qa.a: Nikita could ask, "If I hadn't paid anything yet, would I choose this course today?", and talk it through with a trusted adult or a course advisor before the deadline.

qa.q: How might Leela feel watching the form stay blank?
qa.a: Leela seems worried and frustrated, having named the skipped classes only to see Nikita dig in harder.

grounding: A student who paid a lot for a disappointing course insists it is excellent and will not consider leaving, because admitting doubt would sting.
